column4: A student keeps part of this month's wage in cash to buy textbooks next month. Which function of money does this illustrate?
column5: Medium of exchange|Unit of account|Store of value|Standard of deferred payment
column9: Money as a store of value transfers purchasing power from the present to the future.

column4: Money that has no intrinsic value and is accepted because the government decrees it is called:
column9: Fiat money is established by government decree; commodity money (e.g. gold) has intrinsic value.

column4: Under 100-percent-reserve banking, banks do not affect the money supply.
column9: Each deposit is fully held as reserves, so deposits simply replace currency one-for-one and M is unchanged.

column4: In the model of the money supply, the monetary base $B$ is equal to:
column5: Currency plus demand deposits|Currency plus bank reserves|Bank reserves plus demand deposits|Demand deposits only
column9: B = C + R: the currency held by the public plus the reserves held by banks (high-powered money).

column4: The currency–deposit ratio is $cr = 0.2$ and the reserve–deposit ratio is $rr = 0.1$. Compute the money multiplier $m$.
Suppose $cr = 0.25$, $rr = 0.15$ and the monetary base is $B = 800$ (billions). Compute the money supply $M$ (in billions).
Using $m = \frac{cr+1}{cr+rr}$ with $rr < 1$, an increase in the currency–deposit ratio $cr$ (other things equal):
column5: Raises the money multiplier|Lowers the money multiplier|Leaves the money multiplier unchanged|Has an ambiguous effect on the money multiplier
column9: dm/dcr = (rr − 1)/(cr + rr)^2 < 0: when people hold more currency, fewer reserves support deposit creation.

column4: Which of the following are instruments the Federal Reserve uses to influence the money supply or interest rates? (select all that apply)
column5: Open-market operations|Reserve requirements|Interest paid on reserves|Setting the federal income tax rate|Lending to banks at the discount rate
column9: Tax rates are fiscal policy, set by Congress. The others are monetary policy tools.

column4: When the Fed buys government bonds from the public in an open-market operation, the monetary base falls.
column9: An open-market purchase pays for bonds with new money, so the monetary base rises.

column4: A bank has total assets of 1,000 and bank capital of 50. What is its leverage ratio?
A bank has a leverage ratio of 20. If the value of its assets falls by 2 percent, by what percentage does its bank capital fall? (enter a number of percent, e.g. 15)
column9: Capital is 1/20 of assets, so a 2% fall in assets = 0.02 × 20 = 40% of capital. Leverage magnifies losses.

column4: According to Mankiw's account of 1929–1933, the U.S. money supply fell by more than a quarter mainly because:
column5: The Fed sharply reduced the monetary base|Bank failures raised both the currency–deposit and reserve–deposit ratios|Congress abolished the gold standard|Large gold discoveries reduced the value of money
column9: The monetary base actually rose; bank failures made households hold more currency and banks hold more reserves, so the multiplier collapsed.

column4: After the 2008 financial crisis, the very large increase in the monetary base was matched by a roughly proportional increase in M2.
column9: Banks held most of the new base as excess reserves, so the reserve–deposit ratio rose, the multiplier fell and M2 grew far less than B.

column4: Which of the following are included in M2? (select all that apply)
column5: Currency|Demand deposits|Savings deposits|Small time deposits|Large time deposits|U.S. Treasury bonds held by households
column9: M2 = M1 plus savings deposits, small time deposits and retail money market funds. Large time deposits and Treasury bonds are not in M2.

column4: When a central bank buys large quantities of long-term bonds and other assets to expand the monetary base beyond normal open-market operations, the policy is called ______.
column6: quantitative easing|QE|quantitative easing qe|large-scale asset purchases|large scale asset purchases
column9: Quantitative easing (QE), used by the Fed after 2008 and again in 2020.

column4: If the Fed raises the interest rate it pays on bank reserves, other things equal, this tends to:
column5: Raise the reserve–deposit ratio and reduce the money supply|Lower the reserve–deposit ratio and increase the money supply|Leave the money supply unchanged|Raise the currency–deposit ratio
column9: Holding reserves becomes more attractive, so banks hold more reserves (rr rises), lowering the multiplier and M.

column4: The main purpose of federal deposit insurance is to:
column5: Prevent bank runs by maintaining depositor confidence|Raise the reserve–deposit ratio|Finance the government budget deficit|Fix the price of gold
column9: Insured depositors have no reason to rush to withdraw, which prevents self-fulfilling bank runs.

column4: In a fractional-reserve system where the public holds no currency and every bank keeps a reserve ratio of 0.2, a new deposit of 100 eventually supports a total money supply of how much?
column9: With cr = 0, m = 1/rr = 1/0.2 = 5, so the 100 of reserves supports 5 × 100 = 500.

column4: If the currency–deposit ratio is zero, the money multiplier equals $1/rr$.

Using the money-supply model $M = m \times B$ with $m = \frac{cr+1}{cr+rr}$, explain how a wave of bank runs can reduce the money supply even if the central bank holds the monetary base constant. What can policymakers do about it?
column6: Runs raise cr (households switch deposits to currency) and rr (banks hold precautionary reserves); both lower m, so M falls with B fixed (cf. 1929–33). Remedies: deposit insurance, lender of last resort, expanding B to offset the fall in m.
